case_name: Mercer Gold Corporation (Nevada) v. Mercer Gold Corp. (B.C.)
text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Mercer Gold Corporation (Nevada) v.
Mercer Gold Corp. (B.C.),

2012 BCSC 322

Date: 20120302

Docket:
S116184

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Mercer Gold Corporation (Nevada) (formerly Uranium International
Corp.)

Plaintiff

And

Mercer Gold Corp. (B.C.)

Defendant

And

Mercer Gold Corporation (Nevada) (formerly Uranium International
Corp.),

Gordon Brent Pierce also known as Brent Pierce, Gary Powers,

William (Bill) Thomas, Gerry Jardine and Leonard Braumberger

Defendants by way of Counterclaim

Docket:
S113884

Registry:
Vancouver

Between:

Rahim Jivraj

Plaintiff

And

Mercer Gold Corporation

Defendant

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Greyell

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff Mercer Gold
Corporation (Nevada) (formerly Uranium International Corp.) in Action
No. S1161894 and the Defendant Mercer Gold Corporation in Action
No. S113884:

James
C. MacInnis

Counsel for the Defendant Mercer Gold
Corp. (B.C.) in Action No. S116184 and Rahim Jivraj in Action
No. S113884:

Carey
D. Veinotte

Laura McLeod

Counsel for the Defendants by way of
counterclaim Gary Powers, William (Bill) Thomas and Gerry Jardine in Action
No. S116184:

Sean
O. George

Counsel for the Defendant by way of
counterclaim Gordon Brent Pierce in Action No. S116184:

Daniel
Reid

Place and Date of Hearing:

Vancouver,
B.C.

October
26-28;

November 2-3, 2011

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver,
B.C.

March 2, 2012

[
1
]

On October 26-28 and November 2-3, 2011, this
Court heard a number of applications.  The plaintiff Mercer Gold Corporation
(Nevada) ("Mercer Nevada") applied for orders:  staying Mercer Gold
Corp. B.C.'s ("Mercer BC") amended counterclaim (the "ACC")
filed October 24, 2011; striking out certain portions of the ACC; extending the
time for giving notice to submit a question to arbitration, for injunctive
relief under
s. 20
of the
Commercial Arbitration Act
, R.S.B.C.
1996, c. 55; and for other related orders.  Mercer BC applied to stay
arbitration proceedings commenced by Mercer Nevada.

[
2
]

The defendants by counterclaim Gary Powers
("Powers"), William (Bill) Thomas ("Thomas") and Gerry Jardine
("Jardine") (collectively "the named defendants") applied
pursuant to Rule 9-5(1)(a) of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
, B.C. Reg.
168/2009, O.C. 302/2009,

to strike out portions of Mercer BC's ACC as
disclosing no reasonable cause of action.  Brent Pierce ("Pierce"), a
defendant by counterclaim, applied under Rule 9-5(1)(a),(b) and (d), and Rule
3-7(9) and (18) to strike out portions of the ACC concerning him.

[
3
]

The facts giving rise to the applications are
set out in detail in
Mercer Gold Corporation (Nevada) v. Mercer Gold Corp
(B.C.)
,
2011 BCSC 1664
(“
Mercer #1
”), and I will not repeat them
here.  In brief, the dispute arises out of an Option Agreement (the "Agreement")
between Mercer Nevada and Mercer BC relating to the development of mining
property (the "Property") in Colombia.

Mercer BC purported to
issue default notice and termination of that Agreement in August 2011.  Mercer
Nevada took issue with the validity of the default notice and termination
letter.

[
4
]

In
Mercer #1
, I determined that the
issues raised by the parties were covered by an arbitration clause in the
Agreement.  Although I did not believe it was strictly necessary, I granted
Mercer Nevada an extension of time to file notice of arbitration pursuant to
s. 20 of the
Commercial Arbitration Act
.  I further stayed the
court proceedings pursuant to s. 15 of the
Commercial Arbitration Act
.
Finally, I granted an injunction on terms requested by Mercer Nevada to
preserve the status quo as it existed prior to the default notice and
termination letter pending the conclusion of the arbitral proceedings.

[
5
]

In
Mercer #1
,

I explained that I
would deal with the various applications by the defendants to strike out
portions of the ACC in a separate decision.  This was because the parties had
agreed to a 30-day standstill agreement, pending the decision, and were anxious
that a decision be issued.  I was of the view that the issues raised by the
applications to strike were distinct and could be dealt with separately.  These
reasons address the applications to strike portions of the ACC.

[
6
]

The four named personal defendants were joined
to the main action by Mercer BC when it filed a counterclaim naming, as defendants
by way of counterclaim, the four named personal defendants.

[
7
]

The personal defendants, of course, are not
parties to the Agreement and hence are not directly impacted by the arbitration
except as to the extent they may be called as witnesses and the arbitration
board may make findings concerning their evidence.

[
8
]

It is alleged by Mercer BC that each did,
however, play a significant role as an officer or director of Mercer Nevada at
various periods prior to the default notice:  Pierce was involved from the
outset in negotiating the Agreement with Jivraj; Thomas was, at all material
times, the Chief Financial Officer, Treasurer, Secretary and a director of
Mercer Nevada; Jardine became a director of Mercer BC on May 16, 2011 and
Powers the President and CEO since July 29, 2011.  The allegations by Mercer BC
are that the personal defendants each had a relationship with Pierce of some
standing and that there was a conspiracy involving the personal defendants
prior to their taking positions as directors or officers of Mercer Nevada.

[
9
]

In its ACC, Mercer BC alleges that Mercer Nevada
and each of the named personal defendants were involved in a conspiracy, made
fraudulent or negligent misrepresentations, committed the torts of passing off
and slander of title, and breached various portions of the
Securities Act
,

R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 418.

[
10
]

Mercer Nevada applies pursuant to Rule 9-5(1) to
strike those portions of the ACC that seek damages for diminution of share
value and those that seek damages under the
Securities Act

for secondary
market transactions on the basis that they disclose no reasonable cause of
action.

[
11
]

Pierce applies pursuant to Rule 9-5(1)(a),(b)
and (d) of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
to dismiss the ACC on the
grounds it discloses no reasonable cause of action, is unnecessary, scandalous
and frivolous or vexatious, and is otherwise an abuse of the process of the
court.  Pierce's application is supported by the other named defendants and by
Mercer Nevada insofar as the pleadings relate to allegations against them.

[
12
]

Jardine, Thomas and Powers apply pursuant to
Rule 9-5(1) for orders that those portions of the counterclaim and the ACC
advancing claims of conspiracy, deceit, fraudulent and innocent
misrepresentation, passing off and slander of title be struck out as disclosing
no reasonable cause of action.  Pierce and Mercer Nevada support the
application.

[
13
]

In their respective notices of application, the
applicants argued several other different bases for striking the pleadings.  In
response, Mercer BC amended its pleadings.  Mercer BC takes the position that
the amendments address the issues raised by the applicants.  The applicants
have since abandoned many of the allegations in their respective notices of
application.  These reasons only address those issues that remained outstanding
at the hearing of the matter.

THE LEGAL TEST TO BE APPLIED

[
14
]

Rule 9-5 of the
Rules
reads:

Rule 9-5 — Striking Pleadings

Scandalous,
frivolous or vexatious matters

(1)        At any stage of a proceeding, the
court may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a
pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a)        it
discloses no reasonable claim or defence, as the case may be,

(b)        it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c)        it may
prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing of the proceeding, or

(d)        it is
otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court
may pronounce judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and
may order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
15
]

The principles to be followed by the court on
applications to strike out pleadings were addressed in the often cited case of
Hunt
v. Carey Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959:

(a)       It should be assumed that the facts as stated in the
pleading can be proven;

(b)       The question to be asked whether it is "plain and
obvious" that the plaintiff's claim discloses no reasonable cause of
action in the sense that it is certain to fail because it contains a radical
defect;

(c)        If there is a chance that the plaintiff might succeed,
the plaintiff should not be driven from the judgment seat; and

(d)       The length and complexity of the issues, the novelty of
the cause of action and the potential strength of the defendant's case should
not prevent the claim from proceeding.

[
16
]

Madam Justice Fenlon summarized the applicable
principles recently in
Hundal v. Border Carrier Ltd.
,
2011 BCSC 1703
:

[4]        The principles to be applied in
determining whether a reasonable claim is alleged are as follows:

1.         No evidence is to be considered, only the pleadings: Rule
9-5(2).

2.         The facts alleged are to be taken as proven:
Canadian
Bar Assn. v. British Columbia
(2008),
2008 BCCA 92 (CanLII)
, 76 B.C.L.R. (4th) 48 (C.A.) at para.
37
.

3.         The notice of claim must be read as generously as
possible so as to accommodate any inadequacies in the form of the allegations
which are merely the result of drafting deficiencies:
Evergreen Building
Ltd. v. IBI Leaseholds Ltd.
,
2005 BCSC 1929
at para.
2
.

4.         A pleading should not be struck if it could be amended to
disclose a reasonable claim:
Horton Bay Holdings Ltd. v. Wilks
(1991), 3
C.P.C. (3d) 112 at p. 119
.

5.         It must be plain and obvious that no reasonable cause of
action is disclosed. If there is a chance that the plaintiff might succeed,
then he should not be driven from the judgment seat:
Odhavji Estate v. Woodhouse

(2003),
2003 SCC 69 (CanLII)
, 233 D.L.R. (4th) 193 (S.C.C.) at para.
15
.

6.         The weakness of the case is no reason to strike. The sole
question is whether the plaintiff presents a question fit to be tried:
Citizens
for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C.
(4th) 266 (B.C.S.C.) at para.
37
.

[5]        It
is apparent from this review that the bar is set quite high for the applicant.
Counsel for the defendants submits that the plaintiff’s claim in oppression
does not disclose a reasonable cause of action because Mr. Hundal is
claiming in his personal capacity for wrongs done to the defendant corporation,
Border Carrier Ltd.

DISCUSSION

[
17
]

The principles set out in
Hunt

are to be
strictly followed.  The courts are required to exercise caution before taking a
step which would "drive a person from the judgment seat":
Hundal

at
para.
4
.

[
18
]

There are five main grounds upon which the
parties allege that the allegations in the ACC are bound to fail.  First, the
applicants say that allegations of breaches of the secondary market provisions
of the
Securities Act
are bound to fail because Jivraj's shares
(assigned to Mercer BC) were not acquired in the secondary market but, rather,
were distributed from Mercer Gold's treasury upon execution of the Agreement.  Second,
the applicants say that Mercer BC's claims for damages for diminution of share
value are bound to fail because they were not brought pursuant to a derivative
action.  Third, Jardine, Thomas and Powers say that any allegations of
conspiracy to induce Mercer BC to enter into the Agreement against Jardine and
Powers must fail because they were not directors of Mercer Nevada at the
relevant time.  Fourth, Pierce applies to strike out the pleadings on the basis
that they are so confusing as to be embarrassing.  Finally, Mercer Nevada and
the named personal defendants argue that the ACC ought to be struck because the
matter is within the jurisdiction of the arbitrators.

A.        Secondary
Market Transactions

[
19
]

Mercer BC pleads that certain of the acts and
matters described in the ACC give rise to a civil right of action under Part
16.1 of the
Securities Act
.

[
20
]

In the ACC Mercer BC seeks:

Damages against
Mercer Nevada and the Defendants by Counterclaim pursuant to Par 16.1 of the BC
Act – Civil Liability for Secondary Market Disclosure.

and sets out
its legal basis for such relief:

By virtue of
the acts and matters described in paragraphs 19 to 33, 52 to 54, 57 to 60 and,
66 to 78 herein, Mercer BC has a civil right of action further to the secondary
market liability provisions of the BC Act set forth in Part 16.1 – Civil
Liability for Secondary Market Disclosure and will seek leave of this Court to
prosecute same.

[
21
]

Mercer Nevada takes the position that insofar as
Mercer BC alleges breaches of the
Securities Act
the matters are properly
before the Securities Commission, not through the courts in a civil action.  This
is because the only sections that create civil liability under the
Securities
Act
do not apply to the facts of this case.  Mercer Nevada points out that
Part 16 of the
Securities Act
has no application to Mercer BC's claim.  Further,
Mercer Nevada says that Part 16.1, upon which Mercer BC relies in its pleadings,
is intended to provide damages to shareholders of public companies that suffer
losses arising from the buying or selling of securities when there have been
misrepresentations or non-disclosure by public companies.  Since Mercer BC does
not claim to have either purchased or sold shares in the secondary market,
Mercer Nevada says that Part 16.1 does not apply.

[
22
]

The named defendants, including Pierce, submit
that the secondary market provisions do not apply because Mercer BC has not
pleaded that the shares were bought or sold.  Further, they note that Part 16.1
creates a statutory cause of action that cannot be commenced without leave of
the court.  Since Mercer BC has not sought leave, the named defendants take the
position that the pleadings cannot disclose a reasonable cause of action.  The
named defendants also point out that Mercer BC has not pleaded a specific section
of the
Securities

Act
.  The named defendants rely on
Round v.
MacDonald, Dettweiler & Associates Ltd.
,

2011 BCSC 1416
.

[
23
]

Mercer BC acknowledges it brings its claim
pursuant to s. 140.3 which is contained in Part 16.1 of the
Securities
Act
.  In its submission, although technically leave is required to bring a
claim, the proper response is to stay this portion of the counterclaim rather
than strike it out altogether.

[
24
]

Section 140.3
of the
Securities Act

provides
a statutory cause of action for persons who trade in securities after a person
with actual, implied or apparent authority to act on behalf of the responsible
issuer makes a misrepresentation.  The provision specifically creates presumed
reliance on those misrepresentations.

[
25
]

As noted, s. 104.3 is found within Part 16.1 of
the
Securities Act
,
“Civil Liability for Secondary Market Disclosure”.
In
Round
, Mr. Justice Harris set out the test for leave to be
granted to start an action under this part of the Act.  Specifically, Mr. Justice
Harris concluded that where an interest in shares was not acquired in the
secondary market, no cause of action under Part 16.1 will lie.  He stated:

[59]      MDA argued that a distribution of
shares from a company's treasury to an employee is exempt from Part 16.1 (the
secondary market liability provisions) if the distribution is voluntary. It is
not in dispute that Ms. Round received her entitlement to shares through
her voluntary participation in the Employee Share Purchase Plan.

[60]      The basis of this argument is that
Part 16.1 does not apply to the acquisition of an issuer’s security pursuant to
a distribution that is exempt from s. 61, unless the acquisition is within
a class of prescribed acquisitions: see s. 140.2(b)
.
In other
words, the distribution must meet two conditions. It must be exempt from
s. 61. If it is exempt, it must also not fall within a class of prescribed
acquisitions.

[61]      The first question, therefore, is
whether this distribution is exempt from s. 61. Section 61 provides that
an issuer must not distribute a security unless a prospectus has been filed,
unless an exemption applies. A distribution includes: “(a) a trade in a
security of an issuer that has not been previously issued”: see s. 1(1)
definition of “distribution”. It is not in dispute that Ms. Round’s shares
were a distribution within the meaning of this definition.

[62]      The next aspect of this question
is whether this distribution is exempt from the requirement that a prospectus
be filed.
Section 2.24
of
National Instrument 45-106
Prospectus and
Registration Exemptions
, B.C. Reg. 269/2005 (now replaced by
B.C. Reg.
227/2009
) exempts from the prospectus requirement a distribution “by an issuer
of its own issue... with an employee... if participation in the distribution is
voluntary”. This provision applies to Ms. Round’s acquisition of her
shares. It follows that the distribution of shares to Ms. Round is exempt
from s. 61.

[63]      The second question is whether,
nonetheless, the “acquisition is within a class of prescribed acquisitions”. If
it were, Part 16.1 would apply. It is clear however that the distribution here
does not fall within a class of prescribed acquisitions. The class of
"prescribed acquisitions" referred to in s. 140.2 is set out in

s. 185.3
of the
Securities Rules
, B.C. Reg. 194/97. These
Rules

relate to the resale of securities and takeover bids. The distribution of
shares to Ms. Round does not fall within the class of "prescribed
acquisitions".

[64]      In
the result, the secondary market liability provisions do not apply to confer a
cause of action on Ms. Round in respect of the shares she acquired through
the Plan.

[
26
]

In my view those provisions of the ACC claiming
relief under Part 16.1 must be struck out as disclosing no reasonable cause of
action.  The pleadings do not establish Mercer BC received shares from any
secondary market transaction.  Rather, the evidence is that Mercer BC was
issued shares from the treasury of Mercer Nevada.

[
27
]

It is also fatal to Mercer BC's claim that it
did not obtain leave of the court before making the claim in the ACC.
Section
140.8
of the
Securities Act
provides:

Leave to proceed

140.8

(1) No action may be commenced under
section 140.3
without leave of the
court granted upon motion with notice to each defendant.

(2)        The court may grant leave only
where it is satisfied that

(a)        the
action is being brought in good faith, and

(b)        there
is a reasonable possibility that the action will be resolved at trial in favour
of the plaintiff.

(3)        Upon an application under this
section, the plaintiff and each defendant must serve and file with the court
one or more affidavits setting forth the material facts upon which each intends
to rely.

(4)        If an affidavit is filed with the
court, a person who made the affidavit may be examined on it in accordance with
the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
.

(5)        A
copy of the application for leave to proceed and any affidavits filed with the
court must be sent to the commission when filed.

B.        Derivative
Action

[
28
]

The ACC alleges that Jivraj and his father
transferred all of their shares and assigned their causes of action against
Mercer Nevada to Mercer BC.  As such, Mercer BC claims damages for diminution
of share value on behalf of Jivraj and his father, who hold the restricted
shares issued to Mercer Nevada pursuant to the Agreement.

[
29
]

Mercer Nevada says that to the extent Mercer BC
claims damages from the named defendants for diminution of share price as a
shareholder, it has no cause of action.  Mercer Nevada relies on the rule in
Foss
v. Harbottle
(1843), 67 E.R. 189 (Ch.)
; the company and its shareholders
are different legal entities.  It follows that only the company can sue for
harm done to it.  The proper way for a shareholder to proceed in such a case is
by bringing a derivative action on behalf of the company.

[
30
]

In this respect Mercer Nevada further says that
Mercer BC cannot overcome the rule in
Foss
by pleading unlawful
interference with economic interests because that tort requires an intention to
harm the plaintiff.

[
31
]

Mercer Nevada likewise takes the position that
Mercer BC cannot maintain a claim for diminution in value of the restricted
shares.  In its submission, pursuant to the rule in
Foss
, only a
company, not the individual shareholders, can bring an action for wrongs done
to the company.  As such, it says that since Mercer BC's claim for diminution
in share value is a complaint about a wrong done to the company, Mercer BC's
claim must be brought by Mercer Nevada itself.

[
32
]

The named defendants further say that to avoid
the rule in
Foss v. Harbottle
there must be a relationship between the
shareholder and the wrongdoer that is independent of the relationship which the
shareholder derives through the shareholder’s interest in the company, as well
as a loss separate from that of the company that is causally linked to the
personal wrong done to the plaintiff.  The defendants rely on
Robak
Industries Ltd. v. Gardner
,
2007 BCCA 61
.  The named defendants say that
there is an analogy to the facts in
Robak
insofar as Mercer BC's claim
in conspiracy for the diminution of the value of the restricted shares is, like
the claim in
Robak
, a consequential loss caused by direct damage to the
company rather than the shareholder.

[
33
]

Based on this, the named defendants say that the
conspiracy claims ought to be struck out except for those claims that arise out
of the alleged conspiracy to "take control of the property".

[
34
]

Mercer BC argues
Robak
should be
distinguished, asserting that, in this case, there is an independent cause of
action that has caused harm to the restricted shares.  This, it says, takes the
pleading outside of the rule in
Foss v. Harbottle
.

[
35
]

In my view, the claims asserted by the
plaintiffs and the facts on which those claims were based are similar to those
asserted by Mercer BC in this case.  In
Robak
the plaintiff Lipinski was
the president and a director of Getty (a company involved in mineral
exploration and development).  He and his wholly-owned holding company brought
an action against the respondents alleging, amongst other claims, that the
respondents and others involved had wrongfully planned to seize control of
Getty, entered into a conspiracy to apply "economic duress" to Getty,
engaged in conduct concerning undisclosed insider trading, acted in a bad faith
and in a manner contrary to the best interests of Getty, and made defamatory
statements.  In
Robak
, Robak and Lipinski, as has Mercer BC in this
case, claimed damages which (in
Robak
) were described as including
"loss in the value of ... a substantial interest in the shares of
Getty."  In the present case the claim is for "the diminution in
value of the Restricted Shares received by Mercer BC on or about April 21,
2011".

[
36
]

The Court of Appeal upheld the chamber judge's
conclusion that the impugned portion of the pleadings in
Robak
offended
the rule in
Foss v. Harbottle
.  After reviewing a number of authorities,
including the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in
Hercules Management
Ltd. v. Ernst and Young et al.
,
[1997] 1 S.C.R. 165
, Madam Justice Levine
stated:

[35]      There are good reasons for not
allowing a shareholder to claim the loss in value of its shares where a wrong
has been done to the company. As explained by Laskin J.A. in
Meditrust

(at para. 13); La Forest J. in
Hercules
(at para. 59), and McKenzie J.
in
Rogers
at 78-81 (citing
Prudential Assurance
and
Green v.
Victor Talking Mach. Co.
,
24 F. 2d 378
(1928) (C.A. 2nd Circ.)), the rule
avoids a multiplicity of actions. Further, and consistent with the legal theory
of
Foss v. Harbottle
, the loss in value of shares of a company is a loss
of all of the shareholders, not just one or some of them. There is no logic
that would allow only one shareholder to claim that loss, where the claim
relates to wrongs done to the company, and all of the shareholders have
suffered the loss in value. A single shareholder cannot claim that the loss in
value of the shares,
per se
, is a personal, direct loss.

[36]      The appellants suggest that the
English cases have exposed the underlying principle of
Foss v. Harbottle
,
as interpreted by
Prudential Assurance
, as one of avoiding "double
recovery" for the same loss: once by the company and secondly by the
shareholders: see
Johnson v. Gore Wood
,
per
Lord Bingham, at
para. 44; Lord Cooke at para. 81; Lord Hutton at paras. 97 and 99; Lord Millett
at para. 124.  Thus, if it can be shown that the company cannot sue for
the loss, the shareholder may. The appellants say that Getty cannot sue for the
loss in value of the shares; therefore, the appellants may.

[37]      Double recovery is a consequence
that is avoided by the application of the rule in
Foss v. Harbottle
, but
the jurisprudence does not support the appellants’ argument that it is the
principal reason for its existence. In addition to the reasons for the rule
discussed above, as Lord Hutton and Lord Millett pointed out in
Johnson v.
Gore Wood
, citing
Prudential Assurance
, the rule bars recovery by
one or some shareholders of losses caused by wrongs done to the company, at the
expense of creditors and other shareholders of the company.  (See also:
Gardner

v. Parker
, [2004] 2 BCLC 554 at para. 33 (Eng. C.A.);
Thomas v. D’Arcy
& Ors
, [2005] QCA 68 at para. 11 (Queensland S.C., C.A. Div.).

Summary and Conclusion

[38]      The
appellants’ arguments, based on the consideration of the rule in
Foss v.
Harbottle
in other jurisdictions, does not reveal that the chambers judge
made any error in striking out the portions of the Further Amended Statement of
Claim. She did not apply the wrong test for striking pleadings; she considered
whether the appellants had a reasonable cause of action, including a valid
claim for damages. She applied binding Canadian law, which has been considered
and affirmed in a persuasive judgment of the Ontario Court of Appeal in
Meditrust
.
In both
Rogers
and
Meditrust
, shareholders claimed losses in the
value of their shares as the result of an alleged conspiracy against them
involving wrongs done to the company, and in both cases the claims were
dismissed. The chambers judge did not decide, contrary to the appellants’
arguments, that a shareholder may
never
bring a claim for the diminution
in the value of the shareholder’s shares, but confirmed, by reference to
Hercules

and
Haig
, that a shareholder may have a cause of action for loss in the
value of shares where the shareholder has both an "independent
relationship" with the wrongdoer and an "independent loss" from
that of the company to whom the wrong has been done. She decided that in this
case, the appellants had not shown that they have a cause of action for an
"independent loss" in respect of wrongs done to Getty.  I agree
with her conclusion.

[
37
]

The ACC contains the following paragraphs:

Conspiracy

11.       Mercer BC says that the Defendants by Counterclaim, and
whilst under their direction, the Plaintiff Mercer Nevada, engaged in a
conspiracy, which conspiracy consisted of two parts: first, gain control of the
Property; second, maintain control of a majority or controlling interest of
Mercer Nevada’s stock; and conceal that control from the regulatory authorities
and the other shareholders, including Mercer BC and Jivraj; and, then
manipulate the price of the company’s stock to reap undisclosed profits (known
in securities parlance as a “pump and dump” scheme).

12.       In March and April 2010, Pierce learned from Mercer BC and
Jivraj of the opportunity presented by the Property.  Pierce approached Thomas,
who was an officer and director of Mercer Nevada (known at the time as Uranium
International).  Pierce and Thomas, and by virtue of their control of it,

I have already referred to the principles

Hunt
.  Specifically, assuming that the facts in the
pleadings can be proven, the court must ask whether it is "plain and

action in the sense that it is certain to fail on the basis that it contains a
radical defect.  If there is a chance that the claim may succeed, then the
plaintiff should not be driven from the judgment seat.  Complex issues, the
novelty of a cause of action, and the potential strength of the defendants'

In
Homalco Indian Band

Mr. Justice Smith

described the function of pleadings:

5
The
ultimate function of pleadings is to clearly define the issues of fact and law
to be determined by the court. The issues must be defined for each cause of
action relied upon by the plaintiff. That process is begun by the plaintiff
stating, for each cause, the material facts, that is, those facts necessary for
the purpose of formulating a complete cause of action: Troup v. McPherson
(1965),
1965 CanLII 767 (BC SC)
, 53 W.W.R. 37 (B.C.S.C.) at 39. The defendant, upon seeing the case to
be met, must then respond to the plaintiff's allegations in such a way that the
court will understand from the pleadings what issues of fact and law it will be
called upon to decide.

6
A
useful description of the proper structure of a plea of a cause of action is
set out in J.H. Koffler and A. Reppy, Handbook of Common Law Pleading, (St.
Paul, Minn.: West Publishing Co., 1969) at p. 85:

Of course the
essential elements of any claim of relief or remedial right will vary from
action to action. But, on analysis, the pleader will find that the facts
prescribed by the substantive law as necessary to constitute a cause of action
in a given case, may be classified under three heads: (1) The plaintiff's right
or title; (2) The defendant's wrongful act violating that right or title; (3)
The consequent damage, whether nominal or substantial. And, of course, the
facts constituting the cause of action should be stated with certainty and
precision, and in their natural order, so as to disclose the three elements
essential to every cause of action, to wit, the right, the wrongful act and the
damage.

If the
statement of claim is to serve the ultimate purpose of pleadings, the material
facts of each cause of action relied upon should be set out in the above
manner. As well, they should be stated succinctly and the particulars should
follow and should be identified as such: Gittings v. Caneco Audio-Publishers
Inc. (1988),
1988 CanLII 2832 (BC CA)
, 26 B.C.L.R. (2d) 349 (C.A.) at 353.

[

In my view, the
statement of claim is an embarrassing pleading. It contains much that appears
to be unnecessary. As well, it is constructed in a manner calculated to confuse
the defendants and to make it extremely difficult, if not impossible, to
answer. As a result, it is prejudicial. Any attempt to reform it by striking
out portions and by amending other portions is likely to result in more
confusion as to the real issues. In the interests of all parties, it must be
set aside with leave to the plaintiffs to substitute a statement of claim
prepared in accordance with the principles set out in these reasons: see
Gittings v. Caneco Audio-Publishers Inc., supra, at 352-53.
